summary: Recommends retiring version 2 of the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol and its dependent specifications, and explains why. It recommends moving RFC 1777, 1778, 1779, 1781 and 2559, and the documents they superseded, to Historic status.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo recommends retiring LDAPv2 because implementations do not consistently follow its specification and it lacks important security features. It recommends LDAPv3 instead.

questions: should i implement ldapv2 or ldapv3
why was ldapv2 moved toward historic status
subtitle: Recommends retiring LDAP version 2 because of interoperability and security problems.

tldr.problem: LDAPv2 implementations use behaviors that differ from its specification, and LDAPv2 lacks adequate integrity, confidentiality, and modern authentication support.
tldr.mechanism: The memo recommends moving LDAPv2 and dependent specifications to Historic status and recommends that developers and deployers use LDAPv3 instead.
tldr.outcome: It explains why LDAPv2 should be retired and identifies related documents for Historic status. The unit metadata lists the superseded LDAP documents it obsoletes.

today: RFC 3494 is listed as Informational. It recommends that LDAPv2 and related specifications be moved to Historic status; the unit metadata lists RFCs 1484, 1485, 1487, 1777, 1778, 1779, 1781, and 2559 as obsoleted by this memo.

sections.title: Why LDAPv2 Should Be Retired
sections.content:
LDAPv2 was published as a Draft Standard, but the memo says the specification has several inadequacies. LDAPv3 was published to address them and is technically superior, according to this document.

Existing LDAPv2 implementations often use different character encodings and attribute names from those required by the specification. As a result, a new implementation that follows the written specification may not interoperate with existing systems.
sections.plainLanguage: LDAPv2's written rules and existing implementations do not reliably match. This can prevent independently built systems from working together.

sections.title: Compatibility Problems
sections.content:
The RFC gives examples of differences between the specification and implementations. The specification restricts text to IA5 and T.61, while implementations may use ISO 8859-1, UCS-2, UTF-8, or a local character set.

It also requires a particular attribute name from X.500, while implementations may use the shorter name from the LDAPv3 schema. These differences make it difficult to implement LDAPv2 consistently.
sections.plainLanguage: Implementations may encode text or name attributes differently from the written rules. Systems can then disagree about how to read the same directory information.

sections.title: Security and Recommendation
sections.content:
LDAPv2 provides no data integrity or confidentiality and does not support modern authentication mechanisms such as DIGEST-MD5, Kerberos V, or X.509 public keys. The memo says these features are inadequate for general Internet use.

It recommends that developers not implement LDAPv2 as specified and that deployers use LDAPv3 instead. It also recommends moving LDAPv2 and dependent specifications, including earlier superseded documents, to Historic status.
sections.plainLanguage: LDAPv2 does not protect data from changes or conceal it, and it lacks modern authentication support. The memo recommends using LDAPv3 and retiring LDAPv2 documents.
